newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cambodian prince's bid for home thwarted in HK.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian prince's bid for home thwarted in HK.

text.p: Cambodian authorities on Wednesday blocked a new bid by exiled Prince Norodom Sirivudh to fly home to contest charges of plotting to kill Co-Premier Hun Sen, leaving the prince stranded in Hong Kong for a second day.
"We have given firm instructions to decline any boarding of His Highness Prince Sirivudh," Royal Air Cambodge chairman Vichit Ith told Reuters in the Cambodian capital.
He said the decision was taken out of consideration for the safety of other passengers on Thursday's flight from Hong Kong to Phnom Penh. "We do not want to take any risk."
Sirivudh has been threatened with arrest if he returns to Phnom Penh, and reports from there said the government might send troops to meet any flight which carried him.
Hong Kong's Dragonair airline refused to allow him on its Tuesday flight to Phnom Penh, making it unlikely that Air Cambodge would behave any differently.

"I had an indication from Mr Andre Lim, the (Cambodian) consul here...that Air Cambodge will be in trouble (landing me)... It seems that we cannot even book a reservation," Sirivudh said by telephone from a hotel room in Hong Kong.
Sirivudh later checked out from the airport Regal Hotel and his whereabouts were not known.
The Cambodian consulate was closed for a holiday and officials were not available for comment.
Sirivudh said on Tuesday, after flying into Hong Kong from Germany, that he would persist in attempts to go home and seek a fair trial. He repeated this resolve on Wednesday.
"I just like to stick to (my) legal and my constitutional rights. I am ready to go to jail and I just ask for a review of my trial," he told Reuters.
Sirivudh said Co-Premier Prince Ranariddh and the royalist FUNCINPEC party supported his return. "So I hope that we'll get protection. I don't want to create any confrontation," he said.

A half-brother of King Norodom Sihanouk and a former foreign minister, Sirivudh went into exile in December 1995 after being held for one month on charges of involvement in an alleged plot against the life of Hun Sen.
Hun Sen, who rules in an uneasy coalition with the FUNCINPEC party of Sirivudh's nephew Ranariddh, has refused to back calls for an amnesty and warned last week of violence if the prince returned.
Last December Hun Sen said he would shoot down any plane carrying Sirivudh.

Sirivudh said he did not think he would be killed when he arrived in Cambodia. "I believe in our institutions. We have a monarchy, we have a king, we have a national assembly, we have a royal government."
The Hong Kong government indicated it would not interfere.

"This has nothing to do with the Hong Kong government and this is entirely a matter for the individual to take up with the appropriate parties, be it an airline or authorities of another country," a government spokeswoman told Reuters.
Unconfirmed reports from Phnom Penh said British authorities in Hong Kong were willing to let the prince stay more than a few days but wanted him to return to Europe.
But the spokeswoman would only say that the government had granted Sirivudh "a short period of stay to allow him to rearrange his schedule".
She confirmed authorities would protect Sirivudh, who holds a Cambodian diplomatic passport, until his departure "because of legitimate security concerns, not on the basis of courtesy".
